answer: It began in the U.S. housing market. U.S. house prices, which had doubled since 2000, started falling in 2007, and it became clear that many mortgages made during the boom were of poor quality: borrowers could not keep up their payments, and with falling prices many mortgages exceeded the value of the house, giving an incentive to default. Banks had bundled these mortgages into new securities, repackaged them again and sold them to other banks and investors. Those securities were so complex that their value was nearly impossible to assess, so banks stopped lending to each other. This complexity and opacity turned a housing-price decline into a major financial crisis. Lehman Brothers went bankrupt on September 15, 2008, and the financial crisis quickly became an economic crisis: stock prices collapsed, spending fell, and trade and financial links turned it into a world recession.

Document 1 gives two reasons. First, unemployment directly hurts the welfare of the unemployed, with financial and psychological suffering. When unemployment rises it becomes both more widespread and more painful, because people stay unemployed longer: in the U.S. the mean duration of unemployment rose from 9 weeks on average in 2000-2007 to 33 weeks in 2010. Second, a rising unemployment rate signals that the economy is not using its resources, its workers in particular, efficiently. (Very low unemployment can also be a problem: the economy may be over-using its resources and run into labor shortages.)

By using real GDP instead of nominal GDP. Nominal GDP values final goods at current prices, so it rises when prices rise even if production does not. Real GDP values the quantities of final goods at constant prices, so its changes reflect production only. In the U.S. the weights reflect relative prices and are updated over time: real GDP in chained (2005) dollars. Economic growth is then the growth rate of real GDP, (Y_t - Y_t-1)/Y_t-1. The difference matters: from 1960 to 2010 nominal GDP rose about 28-fold, but real GDP only about 4.7-fold. The rest was price increases.

Badly. World output shrank by 2.3% in 2009 (Table 1-1), after growing 3.2% a year on average in 2000-2007. Advanced economies contracted by 3.7%, by far the lowest annual growth rate since the Great Depression. Emerging and developing economies still grew, by 2.8%, but that was nearly 4 percentage points below their 2000-2007 average of 6.5%. The U.S. crisis had become a world recession.

It jumped. U.S. unemployment rose from 4.6% in 2007 to 5.8% in 2008, 9.3% in 2009 and 9.6% in 2010, close to 10%. No. Growth has to be fast enough. Okun's law (Figure 2-5, U.S. 1960-2010) shows a tight negative relation: each extra 1% of output growth lowers the unemployment rate by about 0.4 percentage points. But it takes growth of about 3% just to keep unemployment constant, because the labor force grows and output per worker rises over time. Growth above about 3% lowers unemployment; positive growth below 3% still raises it. The key to cutting unemployment is a high enough growth rate, and even then the relation holds on average, not exactly every year.

Not always. They move together most of the time: in most years the CPI and GDP-deflator inflation rates differ by less than 1% (Figure 2-4). But they measure different baskets. The GDP deflator is the price of goods produced in the U.S.; the CPI is the price of goods consumed there, including imports. So when import prices jump relative to domestic prices they diverge. In 1979 and 1980 the price of oil doubled and, because the U.S. is a major oil importer, CPI inflation was significantly higher than GDP-deflator inflation.

Before the crisis Euro-area unemployment was already high: 8.5% on average in 2000-2007 (9.6% in 1980-1999), against 5.0% in the U.S. Some politicians blamed overly tight ECB monetary policy, but most economists point to labor-market institutions: strong job protection that deters hiring and generous unemployment insurance that weakens job search. Others note that unemployment was under 4% in countries such as the Netherlands and Denmark despite generous social insurance, so the problem may lie in how protection is implemented. After the crisis unemployment rose to 9.5% in 2009 and 10.1% in 2010. The outturns then show 10.2% in 2011, 11.4% in 2012 and 12.0% in 2013, well above the fall-2011 forecasts of 9.9% for 2011 and 2012.

Chinese exports did slow during the crisis, but the fall in demand was almost fully offset by a major fiscal expansion by the Chinese government, in particular a large increase in public investment. Demand, and so output, kept growing: 9.6% in 2008, 9.2% in 2009 and 10.3% in 2010 (Table 1-4). Behind this growth are very high capital accumulation (investment above 40% of output) and rapid technological progress, helped by foreign firms and joint ventures.

They carried bad mortgages into the banking system in a form nobody could value. Banks that made mortgages bundled them into new securities and sold these to other banks and investors, and the securities were often repackaged again into further securities. Many banks therefore held these securities instead of the mortgages themselves, and the securities were so complex that their value was nearly impossible to assess. When house prices fell and mortgages went bad, no bank knew how exposed the others were, so banks became very reluctant to lend to each other. Unable to borrow and holding assets of uncertain value, many got into trouble. This complexity and opacity is what turned a housing-price decline into a major financial crisis.

Consumption falls. Hit by the drop in housing prices and the collapse in stock prices, and worried about another Great Depression, U.S. households sharply cut their consumption during the crisis. As of 2011, when Document 1 was written, consumers who had seen the value of their housing and financial wealth fall were still cutting consumption, which helped keep the recovery weak.

A recession is a decrease in output: a period of negative real GDP growth (periods of positive growth are expansions). There is no official definition, but the convention is at least two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth. That is why 2001 counts as a (mild) U.S. recession: annual growth was positive that year, but it was negative in each of the first three quarters.
